opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think a lot of the reason that policy debates go badly today isn't that people lack values; it's that the empirical questions underneath them are really hard, and we don't have good ways to resolve them. Take something like the effects of a minimum wage increase, or how a particular criminal justice reform will play out, or what happens to innovation if you change patent law. These involve enormous numbers of interacting causal factors, the data is noisy, and the experiments you'd want to run are often impossible or unethical. So humans end up falling back on ideology, tribal affiliation, and motivated reasoning, because the evidence doesn't force a conclusion.

Now, if you have AI systems that are smarter than humans, and you can run vast numbers of them, a few things change. One is just sheer labor. You could have the equivalent of millions of very capable researchers digging through every dataset, every historical natural experiment, every relevant paper, and cross-checking each other's work. A lot of social science is bottlenecked on the fact that there are only so many careful analysts, and they have limited time.

Second, these systems can be much better calibrated forecasters. We already know from forecasting tournaments that some methods and some people predict geopolitical and economic outcomes much better than pundits do. AI that's trained on making predictions and getting feedback on whether they come true could become extremely good at saying, "If you adopt policy X, here is the probability distribution over outcomes," and building a track record that people can check.

Third, and I think this is underrated, AI can help with the problem of trust and verification. A big reason people reject inconvenient findings is that they suspect the expert is biased or captured. But with AI you can, in principle, do things like have systems trained by different parties with different priors, show that they converge on the same answer, or let anyone query the model, probe its reasoning, and see whether its conclusions hold up under adversarial testing. You can audit a process in a way that's harder with a human committee.

And then there's the possibility of simulating things, at least partially. Better models of economies, of institutions, of how people respond to incentives, which let you test policies before rolling them out to a whole country.

None of that guarantees people will listen, of course. There's a real risk that AI just becomes another weapon for persuasion and propaganda. But the potential is there for a world where a lot of what we currently argue about as if it were a values disagreement turns out to be a factual question that we can actually settle, and then we can focus our disagreements on the genuinely value-laden parts. That would be an enormous improvement in collective decision-making, and it might matter a lot for handling the AI transition itself well.

r001.rationale: It cites forecasting tournaments as evidence that some forecasters outperform pundits, then suggests more capable AI could forecast policy outcomes accurately.

r002.rationale: It discusses distrust of experts and ways to audit AI, but does not say politicians or the public struggle to identify which judgments come from the strongest relevant expertise.

r003.rationale: It connects better fact-finding to improved collective decision-making and handling the AI transition, extending the benefit beyond understanding alone.

r004.rationale: It does not mention vaccine trials, historical trial durations, or accelerated vaccine development.

fable-5.1.text:
Carl Shulman: So I think the natural starting point is to look at what greater intelligence has already done for us on questions like this. If you look at the history of our understanding of economics, of public health, of how to run institutions, a huge amount of the progress has come from a relatively small number of people who were able to reason carefully, gather data, and notice things that other people were missing. And those people were operating under enormous constraints. They had limited time, limited working memory, they could only read a tiny fraction of the relevant literature, and they had their own biases and motivated reasoning that they couldn't fully escape.

Now, when you think about what AI systems could do, there are a few different channels. One is just raw cognitive capacity. You can have a system that has actually read every paper on, say, the effects of minimum wage laws, that has looked at all the natural experiments, that can run the statistical analyses itself and check whether the results hold up under different specifications. Humans can do pieces of that, but no human has actually done all of it, and the people who come closest are a handful of specialists whose time is incredibly scarce.

A second channel is scale and replication. A lot of what makes social science hard is that the experiments are expensive and slow, and there are so many confounders. But if you can have millions of instances of a system that can design better experiments, analyze observational data much more rigorously, build models that actually track the causal structure, and then do that across every domain simultaneously, you start to get a very different picture. You're no longer bottlenecked on a few thousand researchers in each field.

And then there's a third thing, which I think is actually underrated, which is calibration and honesty. A big part of why policy debates are so bad is that the participants are not trying to get the right answer. They're advocates. They're selecting the evidence that supports their side. And even well-meaning people have a very hard time tracking their own track record. So if you have systems that make a lot of forecasts, that get scored on them, where you can actually check which approaches to reasoning about, say, crime policy or education actually predict outcomes, then you can build up a kind of empirical epistemology that we just don't have today. You can see which methods work.

Now, there's an important caveat, which is that these systems can also be used to produce more persuasive propaganda. The same capabilities that let you figure out the truth let you argue convincingly for falsehoods. So whether this actually improves our collective understanding depends a lot on the incentives and the institutions around it. If people want systems that are accurate, and they can verify that accuracy through track records, I think it could be enormously beneficial. If instead the dominant use is to win arguments, then it's much less clear. But the potential for improvement is very large, because the baseline is honestly quite bad. Most of our policy debates are conducted with a tiny fraction of the relevant evidence, by people who aren't that well calibrated, and who have strong incentives not to update.

r001.rationale: The response describes AI forecasts being scored to identify reasoning methods that predict well, but it does not use differences in people's forecasting performance as evidence for greater cognitive capability.

r002.rationale: It says policy participants often advocate for a side and select supportive evidence, but does not say politicians and the public struggle to identify judgments backed by the strongest relevant expertise.

r003.rationale: The response argues that AI could improve understanding of policy questions, but does not state that increased effort toward accurate understanding could extend beyond epistemic progress.

r004.rationale: The response does not mention vaccine trials, historical trial durations, or accelerated vaccine development.

astra-6.text:
Well, I think it helps to distinguish understanding a problem from agreeing on what we want. Greater intelligence doesn’t automatically resolve differences in values. But a lot of disagreement about policy concerns empirical questions: what effects will this intervention have, how will people respond, and what are the alternatives? Those are things where better reasoning and better evidence can help.

Social questions are difficult partly because there are so many interacting factors. You can’t just look at a correlation and assume that you’ve identified a causal relationship. A more capable AI could help us find flaws in an argument, compare competing explanations, and design studies that distinguish between them. It could also bring together knowledge from different fields that individual researchers struggle to master.

And you don’t have to imagine that it produces a single answer that everyone should trust. You could have systems developing arguments and criticizing each other, identifying which assumptions drive their conclusions, and proposing predictions that we can check. That could improve our understanding even when substantial uncertainty remains.

There are limits, of course. Intelligence doesn’t substitute for evidence that you don’t have, and understanding a policy’s consequences doesn’t guarantee that people will choose it. But we already think careful research and reasoning can make progress on these questions. I don’t see a reason to expect those benefits to stop at the level of the most capable humans.

r001.rationale: The response discusses better AI reasoning and evidence, but does not use differences in people's forecasting performance as evidence.

r002.rationale: It does not say that politicians or the public may have difficulty recognizing the strongest relevant expertise.

r003.rationale: It argues that AI could improve understanding, but does not claim that increased cognitive effort could extend beyond epistemic progress.

r004.rationale: The response does not discuss vaccine trials, historical trial durations, or underestimates of development speed.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, difficult social questions often involve a mix of empirical uncertainty and disagreements about values. Greater intelligence doesn’t automatically resolve the disagreements about values, but it can help us understand what follows from different choices.

Take a policy where we’re uncertain about how people will respond. A more capable AI could examine the evidence, identify problems in the studies, develop better models, and suggest experiments that would distinguish competing explanations. It could also trace consequences that are currently too complicated for us to work through, including how a policy interacts with other institutions.

We already think that having more time, more expertise, and better analysis can improve decisions. AI could provide a very large increase in those resources. And it could help people understand one another’s arguments: sometimes an apparent disagreement about values turns out to depend on different factual beliefs.

That doesn’t mean you should accept whatever an AI says. You’d want ways to check its claims, compare competing analyses, and test predictions. But there’s a lot of room to improve our understanding without assuming that intelligence somehow supplies a uniquely correct answer to every political or moral question.

r002.rationale: It does not say politicians or the public may struggle to identify which judgments come from the strongest relevant expertise.

r003.rationale: It connects better analysis to improved decisions, but does not argue that substantially more cognitive effort for accurate understanding could extend beyond epistemic progress.
